questions.stem: What is an AWS Availability Zone?

options.text: One or more isolated data centers within a Region
options.rationale: Each AZ has independent power, networking and connectivity, and sits in a Region with other AZs.

options.text: A geographic area that contains several AWS Regions
options.rationale: It is the other way around: a Region contains several AZs.

options.text: A location that caches content for Amazon CloudFront
options.rationale: That describes an edge location.

options.text: A single rack of servers inside a data center
options.rationale: An AZ is far larger than a rack.

questions.explanation: Regions contain multiple, isolated Availability Zones; edge locations are separate sites used for caching and edge services.

questions.stem: Which statement about AWS Regions is correct?

options.text: Each Region contains exactly one data center
options.rationale: Regions contain multiple Availability Zones, each with one or more data centers.

options.text: Each Region contains multiple Availability Zones
options.rationale: Each Region is a separate geographic area made up of multiple isolated Availability Zones.

options.text: Resources are copied to every Region automatically
options.rationale: Data stays in the Region you choose unless you replicate it.

options.text: Regions and edge locations are the same thing
options.rationale: Edge locations are separate sites used to serve content close to users.

questions.explanation: A Region is a geographic area built from several isolated Availability Zones; edge locations are separate sites, and data stays in a Region unless you copy it elsewhere.

questions.stem: Why should a company deploy its application across multiple Availability Zones?

options.text: To reduce network latency for customers located on other continents
options.rationale: Serving distant users is a reason to use more Regions or edge services.

options.text: To meet laws that require data to stay in one country
options.rationale: Data residency is handled by choosing the Region.

options.text: So the application stays available if one Availability Zone fails
options.rationale: AZs do not share single points of failure, so a multi-AZ design survives the loss of one.

options.text: To get a lower hourly price for Amazon EC2
options.rationale: Spreading across AZs does not reduce instance prices.

questions.explanation: High availability within a Region comes from using more than one Availability Zone.

questions.stem: A company's application must keep running even if an entire AWS Region becomes unavailable. What should the company do?

options.text: Add more instances in the same Availability Zone
options.rationale: Instances in one AZ fail together with that AZ and its Region.

options.text: Move to a larger instance type
options.rationale: Instance size does not protect against a Regional outage.

options.text: Deploy the workload in a second Region
options.rationale: A multi-Region design protects against the loss of a whole Region, which supports disaster recovery.

options.text: Spread instances across two Availability Zones
options.rationale: Multiple AZs protect against the loss of one AZ, but they all sit in the same Region.

questions.explanation: The clue is an entire Region becoming unavailable: multiple Availability Zones protect against an AZ failure, but only a second Region protects against a Regional outage.

questions.stem: A company must keep customer data inside a specific country to comply with local laws. What should it consider when deciding where to deploy?

options.text: Choose an AWS Region located in that country
options.rationale: Data stays in the Region where you store it, so the Region's location addresses data residency.

options.text: Choose the Region with the lowest prices
options.rationale: Price does not satisfy legal residency requirements.

options.text: Store the data at edge locations
options.rationale: Edge locations cache content; they are not where you keep primary data.

options.text: Use any Region as long as an IAM password policy is set
options.rationale: Password policies do not control where data is stored.

questions.explanation: Data sovereignty is one of the main reasons to choose a particular Region.

questions.stem: What are AWS edge locations primarily used for?

options.text: Running Amazon RDS database instances
options.rationale: Databases run in Regions and Availability Zones.

options.text: Caching content close to end users
options.rationale: Edge locations cache content for services such as Amazon CloudFront so users receive it with lower latency.

options.text: Grouping several AWS Regions together
options.rationale: Edge locations do not group Regions.

options.text: Storing AWS Backup vaults for long-term retention
options.rationale: Backup vaults live in Regions.

questions.explanation: Edge locations are sites separate from Regions where CloudFront caches content near users; databases and backup vaults run inside Regions.

questions.stem: Which service gives an application static IP addresses and routes user traffic over the AWS global network to healthy endpoints?

options.text: Amazon CloudFront
options.rationale: CloudFront caches and delivers content from edge locations; it does not give your application static IP addresses.

options.text: Elastic Load Balancing (ELB)
options.rationale: Elastic Load Balancing distributes traffic to targets within a Region rather than routing users across the AWS global network.

options.text: AWS Global Accelerator
options.rationale: Global Accelerator provides static anycast IP addresses and routes traffic over the AWS global network to the nearest healthy endpoint.

options.text: AWS Direct Connect
options.rationale: Direct Connect links an on-premises network to AWS.

questions.explanation: The clue is static IP addresses: Global Accelerator gives fixed entry points on the AWS edge network, while CloudFront speeds up delivery by caching content.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about Availability Zones are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: They are the same as edge locations
options.rationale: Edge locations are separate sites for caching and edge services.

options.text: They are linked by low-latency networking
options.rationale: AZs are connected by redundant, low-latency networks, which makes synchronous replication practical.

options.text: Each Availability Zone is in a different country
options.rationale: AZs in a Region are in the same geographic area.

options.text: They are physically separate within a Region
options.rationale: AZs are many kilometers apart, so a local event such as a fire or flood does not affect the others.

options.text: They share a single power source to reduce costs
options.rationale: Each AZ has independent power.

questions.explanation: Availability Zones do not share single points of failure, which is why multi-AZ designs are highly available.

questions.stem: A company wants a copy of its Amazon S3 data in a Region on another continent for disaster recovery. Which statement is correct?

options.text: AWS copies all data to every Region automatically
options.rationale: AWS does not move your data between Regions.

options.text: All Regions share one storage system
options.rationale: Regions are isolated from each other.

options.text: The company must configure replication itself
options.rationale: Data stays in its Region until you copy it, for example with S3 Cross-Region Replication.

options.text: Edge locations keep backups of S3 buckets
options.rationale: Edge locations cache content; they are not backup storage.

questions.explanation: Data stays in the Region where you store it, which supports data sovereignty; copying it to another Region for disaster recovery is an explicit choice, such as S3 Cross-Region Replication.

questions.stem: A company runs its web application in one AWS Region in North America. Users in Asia report slow response times. Which approach reduces latency for those users?

options.text: Spread the instances across more Availability Zones
options.rationale: AZs are all in the same Region, so users in Asia are still far away.

options.text: Deploy the application in a Region in Asia
options.rationale: Running the application in a Region close to its users shortens the network distance to them.

options.text: Switch to a larger Amazon EC2 instance type
options.rationale: A bigger instance adds capacity but does not shorten the distance to distant users.

options.text: Purchase Reserved Instances for the servers
options.rationale: Reserved Instances lower cost; they do not change latency.

questions.explanation: The clue is users far from the only Region: low latency for end users is a reason to use multiple Regions, while more Availability Zones improve availability within one Region.

questions.stem: Which TWO AWS services use edge locations to serve users with low latency? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Amazon RDS
options.rationale: RDS databases run in Regions and Availability Zones, not at edge locations.

options.text: Amazon CloudFront
options.rationale: CloudFront caches and delivers content from edge locations close to users.

options.text: AWS Batch
options.rationale: AWS Batch runs batch jobs on compute in a Region.

options.text: Amazon Route 53
options.rationale: Route 53 answers DNS queries from a global network of edge locations.

options.text: Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)
options.rationale: EBS volumes live in one Availability Zone and attach to EC2 instances there.

questions.explanation: Edge locations are sites separate from Regions that bring cached content and DNS answers close to users; databases, block storage and batch jobs run inside Regions.
